title: Burst-aware batching and cache-tolerance playbook for onboarding evals
content:
Purpose:
This playbook captures a focused set of experiments and heuristics to evaluate model variants during onboarding when the workload exhibits bursty arrival patterns. Goal: produce repeatable tradeoff curves (latency vs cost vs quality) that explicitly include burst tolerance (ability to absorb short spikes) as a first-class dimension.

Background and motivation:
- Standard batching + prefix caching evaluations assume relatively steady QPS. In many prod apps (chat widgets, search surge, marketing blasts) traffic is spiky: short periods (1–30s) of high arrival rate followed by lower baseline.
- A model profile that performs well at steady throughput can still cause tail latency spikes or high cost under bursts if batching windows, max_concurrency, or cache admission thresholds are wrong.
- We need a small, reproducible experiment matrix to quantify how different serving knobs change: P95/P99 latency, token cost per request, and output quality (using our promptset evals).

Experiment design (summary):
- Workload generator: synthetic trace with three modes: baseline (5 rps), micro-burst (50 rps for 2s), macro-burst (200 rps for 10s). Repeat cycles for 30 minutes to get stable tail statistics.
- Models: onboarding candidates M-A (fp16 baseline), M-A-q4 (quantized q4), M-B (smaller architecture), M-B-q4.
- Promptset: 120 prompts sampled from onboarding promptset_v2 (mix of short/medium/long). We annotate each prompt with expected token-length bucket (S < 32, M 32–128, L 128–512).
- Knobs to sweep: batching latency window (batch_wait_ms=1,5,10,25,50), max_batch_size (8,32,128), cache_admission_threshold (cache_len_ratio 0.0, 0.25, 0.5), max_tokens cap per request (default, -20%, +20%), concurrency limit per-worker (1,2,4).
- Measurements: P50/P90/P95/P99 generation latency, tokens/sec throughput, average cost per request (model token-cost * tokens), and quality metrics: BLEU-like and our proprietary semantic score (SQS) computed against human-labeled expected outputs. Also track #cache_hits, average batch size, and number of fallback events (requests routed to smaller model due to saturation).

Run plan and data collection notes:
- Each configuration runs for 30 minutes with same seed for request ordering to ensure comparability. Warm-up first 5 minutes (discard). Use isolated Dedicated pool instance to avoid noisy neighbors.
- Logging: request-level JSON with timestamps, batch_id, worker_id, model_variant, tokens_in, tokens_out, latency_ms, cache_hit (bool), quality_score. Aggregate hourly for charts.
- Sanity checks: CPU/GPU utilization, kernel stalls, memory pressure, and queue lengths. Capture snapshot of KV cache size and eviction rate.

Representative results (excerpt):
- Key observation 1: Increasing batch_wait_ms from 5 -> 25 ms reduced per-token cost by ~18% during baseline, but in micro-bursts P95 increased by 40–60ms and P99 doubled. For M-A-q4, the cost savings were slightly higher but tail latency penalty larger because quantized kernels had higher variance under fully-saturated queues.
- Key observation 2: Max_batch_size ceiling (128) helped throughput during macro-bursts but led to more fallback events when combined with concurrency limit 4; smaller models (M-B) absorbed fallbacks with acceptable quality degradation (~2.8 SQS points), preventing P99 outages.
- Key observation 3: Cache admission threshold at 0.5 (only cache prompts where prefix has >=50% token overlap with cached keys) delivered a good tradeoff: cache hit rate dropped ~12% vs permissive caching but eviction churn reduced 3x, improving P99 during long bursts.

Example table (aggregated, single-cycle):
- Config A: batch_wait=5ms, max_batch=32, cache_thresh=0.0, max_tokens=default, concurrency=2 -> P95=210ms, P99=480ms, avg_cost=$0.014, SQS=86.3, cache_hit=42%, avg_batch=18
- Config B: batch_wait=25ms, max_batch=128, cache_thresh=0.5, max_tokens=-20%, concurrency=1 -> P95=260ms, P99=820ms, avg_cost=$0.011, SQS=85.7, cache_hit=30%, avg_batch=64
- Config C (safe): batch_wait=10ms, max_batch=32, cache_thresh=0.5, max_tokens=default, concurrency=2 -> P95=225ms, P99=520ms, avg_cost=$0.0125, SQS=86.0, cache_hit=35%, avg_batch=28

Interpretation and heuristics (playbook):
1) Burst-tolerant defaults: prefer slightly lower batch_wait (5–10 ms) and moderate max_batch_size (32) for customer-facing interactive apps. This keeps P99 bounded while preserving most batching gains.
2) Cache admission: conservative cache admission (>=0.5) for models with large KV caches to avoid churn during bursts. If cache key distribution is narrow (many repeated prefixes), lower threshold is fine.
3) Concurrency: single-worker concurrency (1) reduces queuing variance and thus tail latency at cost of some throughput elasticity; prefer concurrency=1 for strict P99 SLOs, concurrency>1 for throughput-first backends (e.g., offline batch).
4) Quantization: q4 reduces cost but increases variance under heavy bursts on some GPUs—run a short stress test to validate for each GPU family.
5) Fallback policy: enable automatic fallback to smaller model when queue depth or estimated completion time exceeds threshold (example: expected latency > 1.5 * P95 baseline). Track quality regression and cap fallback rate to 5% of requests per minute for critical paths.

Quality tradeoffs and gating:
- Establish Q-gate: onboarding is green if SQS drop <= 3 points relative to reference and P99 increase <= 1.5x baseline for expected burst profile. If cost savings > 20% but SQS drop > 3, escalate to model owner for review.

Open questions / unresolved items:
- How to parameterize burst patterns per-customer? We used a 2s/10s burst patterns; need to build a small library of canonical traces (chat, search, email send) and surface these in Console as presets.
- Can we instrument adaptive batch_wait that short-circuits when queue growth is above a threshold? Prototyping idea: algorithmic early flush when inflight queue > X. (Priya to prototype).
- How much longer-term value from cache admission ML? Could learn threshold per-prefix. High complexity — deprioritize unless cache eviction rates indicate severe churn.

Action items and owners:
- Run full sweep across all onboarding models for EU and US regions (Liam) — target complete by 2025-11-30.
- Implement stress test harness that can replay synthetic trace library (Diego) — prototype by 2025-11-12.
- Add burst-presets to Console rollout UI and expose batch_wait and cache_admission sliders to SREs (Product/Console eng) — design doc needed.

Notes-to-self / working thoughts:
- We should avoid conflating average cost numbers with per-request cost in bursts — include percentiles of cost per minute.
- Remember to attach raw request logs and GPU telemetry when filing a PR for the onboarding report.
- Consider a short experiment where fallback routing includes a very small ensemble (primary + warmed small model) to avoid quality cliffs.

Appendix: quick checklist for onboarding runs
- [ ] Choose canonical trace (chat/search/email)
- [ ] Select promptset buckets (S/M/L) and seed
- [ ] Decide knob grid (batch_wait, max_batch, cache_thresh, concurrency)
- [ ] Reserve dedicated pool / isolate run
- [ ] Warm-up 5m, run 30m, collect logs
- [ ] Produce P50/P90/P95/P99 latency and cost curves, SQS delta, cache stats
- [ ] Create short recommendation (safe/default/cost-optimized)

End of playbook (draft).

Feedback welcome — this is intentionally pragmatic, focused on rapid repeatable signals rather than perfect modeling.
